import Mathlib

/-!
# The Lorentz form of signature `(n,1)`, its integral automorphisms, and the reflection move

This file sets up the general framework in which the Berggren tree of primitive Pythagorean
triples and its higher–dimensional analogues live:

* `lorentzJ n`   — the Gram matrix `diag(1,…,1,-1)` of the form `x₁²+…+xₙ² − y²`;
* `lorentzQ n v` — the form itself;
* `NullCone n`   — its integral null cone (`= ` Pythagorean `n`-tuples);
* `IsIntegralLorentz n M` — the integral automorphisms of the form.

Main results.

* `lorentzQ_mulVec` : integral Lorentz matrices preserve the form, hence the null cone
  (`IsIntegralLorentz.mapsTo_nullCone`).
* `IsIntegralLorentz.det_sq` : such matrices have determinant `±1`.
* `lorentz_move_height_bound` : the *sharp* growth constant of the reflection move in the
  all-ones vector: the height is multiplied by at most `(√n+1)/(√n−1)`.  For `n = 2` this is
  `3+2√2 = (1+√2)²`, the square of the silver ratio (Berggren); for `n = 3` it is `2+√3`.
* `refl_not_integral_of_four_le` : the all-ones reflection is *not* integral for `n ≥ 4`,
  so the Berggren mechanism only exists in dimensions `n = 2, 3`.
-/

namespace HigherPythagorean

open Matrix Finset

section Form

variable (n : ℕ)

/-- Gram matrix of the Lorentz form of signature `(n,1)`: `diag(1,…,1,-1)`. -/
def lorentzJ : Matrix (Fin (n + 1)) (Fin (n + 1)) ℤ :=
  Matrix.diagonal fun i => if i = Fin.last n then -1 else 1

/-- The Lorentz quadratic form `q(v) = v ⬝ J ⬝ v = x₁²+…+xₙ² − y²`. -/
def lorentzQ (v : Fin (n + 1) → ℤ) : ℤ := v ⬝ᵥ (lorentzJ n *ᵥ v)

/-- The integral null cone of the Lorentz form: solutions of `x₁²+…+xₙ² = y²`. -/
def NullCone : Set (Fin (n + 1) → ℤ) := {v | lorentzQ n v = 0}

variable {n}

lemma lorentzJ_transpose : (lorentzJ n)ᵀ = lorentzJ n := by
  simp [lorentzJ, Matrix.diagonal_transpose]

lemma lorentzQ_eq_sum (v : Fin (n + 1) → ℤ) :
    lorentzQ n v = (∑ i : Fin n, (v i.castSucc) ^ 2) - (v (Fin.last n)) ^ 2 := by
  classical
  have h : lorentzQ n v = ∑ i : Fin (n + 1), (if i = Fin.last n then -(v i) ^ 2 else (v i) ^ 2) := by
    simp only [lorentzQ, dotProduct, lorentzJ, mulVec_diagonal]
    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    intro i _
    by_cases hi : i = Fin.last n <;> simp [hi, sq]
  rw [h, Fin.sum_univ_castSucc]
  simp [Fin.castSucc_lt_last, Fin.ne_of_lt]
  ring

/-- Membership in the null cone, written out. -/
lemma mem_nullCone_iff (v : Fin (n + 1) → ℤ) :
    v ∈ NullCone n ↔ (∑ i : Fin n, (v i.castSucc) ^ 2) = (v (Fin.last n)) ^ 2 := by
  simp [NullCone, lorentzQ_eq_sum, sub_eq_zero]

end Form

section Automorphisms

variable {n : ℕ}

/-- An integral automorphism of the Lorentz form: `Mᵀ J M = J`. -/
def IsIntegralLorentz (M : Matrix (Fin (n + 1)) (Fin (n + 1)) ℤ) : Prop :=
  Mᵀ * lorentzJ n * M = lorentzJ n

lemma isIntegralLorentz_one : IsIntegralLorentz (1 : Matrix (Fin (n + 1)) (Fin (n + 1)) ℤ) := by
  simp [IsIntegralLorentz]

lemma IsIntegralLorentz.mul {M N : Matrix (Fin (n + 1)) (Fin (n + 1)) ℤ}

  unfold IsIntegralLorentz at *
  calc (M * N)ᵀ * lorentzJ n * (M * N) = Nᵀ * (Mᵀ * lorentzJ n * M) * N := by
        rw [Matrix.transpose_mul]; noncomm_ring
    _ = Nᵀ * lorentzJ n * N := by rw [hM]
    _ = lorentzJ n := hN

lemma lorentzQ_mulVec {M : Matrix (Fin (n + 1)) (Fin (n + 1)) ℤ} (hM : IsIntegralLorentz M)

  have h1 : M *ᵥ v = v ᵥ* Mᵀ := by rw [Matrix.vecMul_transpose]

      = (M *ᵥ v) ⬝ᵥ (lorentzJ n *ᵥ (M *ᵥ v)) := rfl
    _ = ((M *ᵥ v) ᵥ* lorentzJ n) ⬝ᵥ (M *ᵥ v) := dotProduct_mulVec _ _ _
    _ = (((M *ᵥ v) ᵥ* lorentzJ n) ᵥ* M) ⬝ᵥ v := dotProduct_mulVec _ _ _
    _ = ((v ᵥ* Mᵀ) ᵥ* lorentzJ n ᵥ* M) ⬝ᵥ v := by rw [h1]
    _ = (v ᵥ* (Mᵀ * lorentzJ n * M)) ⬝ᵥ v := by

lemma IsIntegralLorentz.mapsTo_nullCone {M : Matrix (Fin (n + 1)) (Fin (n + 1)) ℤ}

  classical
  rw [lorentzJ, Matrix.det_diagonal, Fin.prod_univ_castSucc]
  simp [Fin.ne_of_lt, Fin.castSucc_lt_last]

  | swap23 {a b c d : ℤ} : Reach a b c d → Reach a c b d
  | refl {a b c d : ℤ} : Reach a b c d →
      Reach (a - qk a b c d) (b - qk a b c d) (c - qk a b c d) (d - qk a b c d)

theorem Reach.neg2 {a b c d : ℤ} (h : Reach a b c d) : Reach a (-b) c d :=
  ((h.swap12).neg).swap12

theorem Reach.neg3 {a b c d : ℤ} (h : Reach a b c d) : Reach a b (-c) d :=
  ((h.swap23).neg2).swap23

theorem reach_of_abs {a b c d : ℤ} (h : Reach |a| |b| |c| d) : Reach a b c d := by
  rcases abs_choice a with ha | ha <;> rcases abs_choice b with hb | hb <;>
    rcases abs_choice c with hc | hc <;> rw [ha, hb, hc] at h <;>
    first
      | exact h
      | simpa using h.neg
      | simpa using h.neg2
      | simpa using h.neg3
      | simpa using h.neg.neg2
      | simpa using h.neg.neg3
      | simpa using h.neg2.neg3
      | simpa using h.neg.neg2.neg3

/-- **Soundness**: every reachable quadruple is a primitive Pythagorean quadruple. -/
theorem reach_sound {a b c d : ℤ} (h : Reach a b c d) : IsPrimQuad a b c d := by
  induction h with
  | root => exact ⟨by unfold IsPythQuadruple; ring, by decide⟩
  | neg h ih =>
      obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := ih
      refine ⟨?_, by rw [content_neg]; exact h2⟩
      unfold IsPythQuadruple at h1 ⊢; linear_combination h1
  | swap12 h ih =>
      obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := ih
      refine ⟨?_, by rw [content_swap12]; exact h2⟩
      unfold IsPythQuadruple at h1 ⊢; linear_combination h1
  | swap23 h ih =>
      obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := ih
      refine ⟨?_, by rw [content_swap23]; exact h2⟩
      unfold IsPythQuadruple at h1 ⊢; linear_combination h1
  | refl h ih => exact ⟨qmove_pyth ih.1, by rw [content_move]; exact ih.2⟩

/-! ## Descent -/

theorem height_one_aux {t d : ℤ} (ht : t = d) (hd : 0 < d) (h : content 0 0 t d = 1) : d = 1 := by
  subst ht
  rw [content_zero_zero] at h
  omega

/-- If all three pairwise products of the space coordinates vanish, primitivity forces the
degenerate quadruple `(1,0,0,1)` up to permutation, i.e. height one. -/
theorem height_one_of_degenerate {a b c d : ℤ} (ha : 0 ≤ a) (hb : 0 ≤ b) (hc : 0 ≤ c) (hd : 0 < d)
    (h : IsPythQuadruple a b c d) (hab : a * b = 0) (hbc : b * c = 0) (hac : a * c = 0)
    (hcont : content a b c d = 1) : d = 1 := by
  unfold IsPythQuadruple at h
  have key : ∀ t : ℤ, 0 ≤ t → t ^ 2 = d ^ 2 → t = d := by
    intro t ht h2; nlinarith
  rcases mul_eq_zero.mp hab with ha0 | hb0
  · rcases mul_eq_zero.mp hbc with hb0 | hc0
    · -- a = 0, b = 0, so c = d
      have hcd : c = d := key c hc (by rw [ha0, hb0] at h; linarith)
      refine height_one_aux hcd hd ?_
      rw [ha0, hb0] at hcont; exact hcont
    · -- a = 0, c = 0, so b = d
      have hbd : b = d := key b hb (by rw [ha0, hc0] at h; linarith)
      refine height_one_aux hbd hd ?_
      rw [ha0, hc0] at hcont
      rw [content_swap23]; exact hcont
  · rcases mul_eq_zero.mp hac with ha0 | hc0
    · -- b = 0, a = 0, so c = d
      have hcd : c = d := key c hc (by rw [ha0, hb0] at h; linarith)
      refine height_one_aux hcd hd ?_
      rw [ha0, hb0] at hcont; exact hcont
    · -- b = 0, c = 0, so a = d
      have had : a = d := key a ha (by rw [hb0, hc0] at h; linarith)
      refine height_one_aux had hd ?_
      rw [hb0, hc0] at hcont
      rw [content_swap23, content_swap12]; exact hcont

/-- The shift `k = a+b+c−d` is strictly positive for a primitive quadruple of height `> 1`. -/
theorem qk_pos {a b c d : ℤ} (ha : 0 ≤ a) (hb : 0 ≤ b) (hc : 0 ≤ c) (hd : 1 < d)
    (h : IsPythQuadruple a b c d) (hcont : content a b c d = 1) : 0 < qk a b c d := by
  unfold qk
  by_contra hcon
  push_neg at hcon
  have hpyth := h
  unfold IsPythQuadruple at hpyth
  have hsum : a + b + c ≤ d := by linarith
  have hab : a * b = 0 := by nlinarith [mul_nonneg ha hb, mul_nonneg hb hc, mul_nonneg ha hc]
  have hbc : b * c = 0 := by nlinarith [mul_nonneg ha hb, mul_nonneg hb hc, mul_nonneg ha hc]
  have hac : a * c = 0 := by nlinarith [mul_nonneg ha hb, mul_nonneg hb hc, mul_nonneg ha hc]
  have := height_one_of_degenerate ha hb hc (by linarith) h hab hbc hac hcont
  omega

/-- The descended height `d − k = 2d − (a+b+c)` is still positive. -/
theorem sub_qk_pos {a b c d : ℤ} (ha : 0 ≤ a) (hb : 0 ≤ b) (hc : 0 ≤ c) (hd : 0 < d)
    (h : IsPythQuadruple a b c d) : 0 < d - qk a b c d := by
  unfold IsPythQuadruple at h
  unfold qk
  nlinarith [sq_nonneg (a - b), sq_nonneg (b - c), sq_nonneg (a - c), sq_nonneg (a + b + c - 2 * d)]

/-- **Completeness / connectivity.** Every primitive Pythagorean quadruple with non-negative
space coordinates and positive height is reachable from the root `(1,0,0,1)`.  This is the
three-dimensional analogue of Berggren's theorem. -/
theorem reach_of_prim : ∀ (N : ℕ) (a b c d : ℤ), d.toNat ≤ N → 0 ≤ a → 0 ≤ b → 0 ≤ c → 0 < d →
    IsPythQuadruple a b c d → content a b c d = 1 → Reach a b c d := by
  intro N
  induction N with
  | zero => intro a b c d hN _ _ _ hd _ _; omega
  | succ N ih =>
      intro a b c d hN ha hb hc hd h hcont
      rcases eq_or_lt_of_le (show (1 : ℤ) ≤ d by omega) with hd1 | hd1
      · -- base case: height one
        subst hd1
        have h' : a ^ 2 + b ^ 2 + c ^ 2 = 1 := by unfold IsPythQuadruple at h; linarith [h]
        have ha1 : a ≤ 1 := by nlinarith
        have hb1 : b ≤ 1 := by nlinarith
        have hc1 : c ≤ 1 := by nlinarith
        have hcase : (a = 1 ∧ b = 0 ∧ c = 0) ∨ (a = 0 ∧ b = 1 ∧ c = 0) ∨
            (a = 0 ∧ b = 0 ∧ c = 1) := by
          interval_cases a <;> interval_cases b <;> interval_cases c <;> simp_all
        rcases hcase with ⟨rfl, rfl, rfl⟩ | ⟨rfl, rfl, rfl⟩ | ⟨rfl, rfl, rfl⟩
        · exact Reach.root
        · exact Reach.root.swap12
        · exact Reach.root.swap12.swap23
      · -- descent step
        have hkpos : 0 < qk a b c d := qk_pos ha hb hc hd1 h hcont
        have hdk : 0 < d - qk a b c d := sub_qk_pos ha hb hc hd h
        have hmove : IsPythQuadruple (a - qk a b c d) (b - qk a b c d) (c - qk a b c d)
            (d - qk a b c d) := qmove_pyth h
        have habs : IsPythQuadruple |a - qk a b c d| |b - qk a b c d| |c - qk a b c d|
            (d - qk a b c d) := by
          unfold IsPythQuadruple at hmove ⊢
          rw [sq_abs, sq_abs, sq_abs]; exact hmove
        have hc2 : content |a - qk a b c d| |b - qk a b c d| |c - qk a b c d|
            (d - qk a b c d) = 1 := by
          rw [content_abs3, content_move]; exact hcont
        have hsmall : (d - qk a b c d).toNat ≤ N := by omega
        have hR := ih |a - qk a b c d| |b - qk a b c d| |c - qk a b c d| (d - qk a b c d)
          hsmall (abs_nonneg _) (abs_nonneg _) (abs_nonneg _) hdk habs hc2
        have hback := (reach_of_abs hR).refl
        rw [qk_move a b c d] at hback
        have e : ∀ x : ℤ, x - qk a b c d - -qk a b c d = x := by intro x; ring
        simp only [e] at hback
        exact hback

/-- Reachability characterises primitive Pythagorean quadruples in the positive cone. -/
theorem reach_iff_prim {a b c d : ℤ} (ha : 0 ≤ a) (hb : 0 ≤ b) (hc : 0 ≤ c) (hd : 0 < d) :
    Reach a b c d ↔ IsPrimQuad a b c d := by
  refine ⟨reach_sound, ?_⟩
  rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩
  exact reach_of_prim d.toNat a b c d le_rfl ha hb hc hd h1 h2

end HigherPythagorean

# Computational Evidence — Higher-Dimensional Pythagorean Trees

All computations below were exploratory (Python, exact integer arithmetic). Every claim that
is *asserted* in this project is separately proved in Lean 4 (`Catalog/Shared/HigherPythagorean/`);
the data here only motivated the theorem statements.

## 1. The setting

For the Lorentz form `q(x₁,…,xₙ, y) = x₁² + … + xₙ² − y²` let `r = (1,…,1;1)`, so `q(r) = n − 1`.
The reflection in `r` is

    s_r(v) = v − (2·B(v,r)/(n−1))·r,     B(v,r) = x₁+…+xₙ − y.

* `n = 2` : `q(r) = 1`, `s_r(a,b,c) = (a−2k, b−2k, c−2k)` with `k = a+b−c` — composed with the four
  sign changes these are exactly Berggren's three moves.
* `n = 3` : `q(r) = 2`, `s_r(a,b,c,d) = (a−k, b−k, c−k, d−k)` with `k = a+b+c−d`. Still integral.
* `n ≥ 4` : `2/(n−1) ∉ ℤ`, so `s_r` is **not** an integral map. (Proved: `refl_not_integral_of_four_le`.)

A *descent* from a node is a sign pattern `ε ∈ {±1}ⁿ` such that the move applied to
`(ε₁x₁,…,εₙxₙ, y)` strictly decreases the height `y` (and keeps it positive).

## 2. Triples (n = 2): exactly one descent — a genuine tree

All 71 primitive triples with legs < 400 were enumerated. Distribution of the number of
distinct decreasing neighbours:

| #descents | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| count | 0 | **71** | 0 |

Unique parent for every node ⇒ the Berggren graph is a tree. Proved in Lean:
`triple_unique_descent_sign` (only `ε = (+,+)` can decrease) and `triple_plus_descent_pos`.

## 3. Quadruples (n = 3): up to two descents — **not** a tree

All 348 primitive reduced quadruples `0 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ c`, `d ≤ 80`, `gcd = 1` were enumerated.
Distribution of the number of distinct decreasing neighbours:

| #descents | 0 | 1 | 2 | ≥3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| count | 1 (the root `(0,0,1,1)`) | 151 | **196** | 0 |

So the majority of nodes have **two** parents: the height-descent structure on Pythagorean
quadruples is a connected graph with many cycles, not a tree. Both facts were then proved:

* never more than two descents: `quad_at_most_two_descents` (a two-minus pattern can never
  descend, and two distinct one-minus patterns cannot both descend);
* two descents occur infinitely often: `quad_two_parents_family`, the family
  `(1, 2m, 2m², 2m²+1)`, `m ≥ 2`.

First members of the family and their two parents (heights in brackets):

| node | parent A | parent B |
|---|---|---|
| (1,4,8,9)   | (3,0,4,5)     [5]  | (3,2,6,7)      [7]  |
| (1,6,18,19) | (5,0,12,13)   [13] | (5,2,14,15)    [15] |
| (1,8,32,33) | (7,0,24,25)   [25] | (7,2,26,27)    [27] |
| (1,10,50,51)| (9,0,40,41)   [41] | (9,2,42,43)    [43] |

(The heights of the two parents differ by exactly 2 for the whole family; the general formulas
are `2m²−2m+1` and `2m²−2m+3`.)

## 4. Connectivity / completeness

For every one of the 348 enumerated primitive quadruples, iterating the all-plus move
terminates at `(0,0,1,1)` (max 200 iterations allowed; all terminated). This is the
computational shadow of the Lean theorem `reach_of_prim`: *every* primitive Pythagorean
quadruple with non-negative entries lies in the orbit of `(1,0,0,1)` under the group generated
by the reflection `s_r`, the coordinate sign changes and the coordinate permutations.

## 5. Growth constants

Maximal one-step expansion factor of the height over the real null cone
(`ε = (−1,…,−1)`, `xᵢ = d/√n`):

| n | expansion factor | value | remark |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | `(√2+1)/(√2−1) = 3+2√2` | 5.828… | `= (1+√2)²`, silver-ratio square; fundamental norm-1 unit of ℤ[√2] |
| 3 | `(√3+1)/(√3−1) = 2+√3`  | 3.732… | fundamental norm-1 unit of ℤ[√3] |
| n | `(√n+1)/(√n−1)`          | → 1    | proved in general (`lorentz_move_height_bound`) |

The general bound and its sharpness at `n = 3` are theorems
(`lorentz_move_height_bound`, `quad_growth_bound_sharp`).

## 6. Sequence lookup

The counts of primitive quadruples by height are the well-studied sequence of primitive
Pythagorean quadruples; no new OEIS entry is claimed here, and no numerical claim in this
project rests on an OEIS identification.

# Summary of changes for run 1a02bead-fd87-49fa-9f95-ca4eb5bd4872
## Higher-Dimensional Pythagorean Trees — completed

All Lean sources are in `Catalog/Shared/HigherPythagorean/` (`LorentzCore.lean`, `QuadrupleTree.lean`, `BranchingContrast.lean`, `HarmonicLaw.lean`, `BerggrenBridge.lean`, `QuadrupleGroupoid.lean`, `HyperbolicBoundary.lean`, `CanonicalTree.lean`, ~1650 lines). `lake build CatalogShared` completes successfully; a search confirms **no `sorry` anywhere** in these files, and the main theorems depend only on the standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`. The files build on the existing catalog definitions (`IsPythQuadruple`, the Berggren matrices `B₁_mat/B₂_mat/B₃_mat` and moves `bergA/bergB/bergC`, `QLor`) rather than re-inventing them.

### What was set up
The null cone of the (n+1)-dimensional Lorentz form and the reflection `s_r(v) = v − (2B(v,r)/(n−1))·r` in the all-ones vector `r = (1,…,1;1)`, `q(r) = n−1`.

### Positive results (all proved)
- **Dimensional classification.** The all-ones reflection is integral exactly for n = 2 and n = 3; for n ≥ 4 the coefficient `2/(n−1)` is not an integer (`refl_not_integral_of_four_le`), with a concrete dimension-4 null vector pushed off the lattice.
- **n = 2 recovers Berggren exactly.** The reflection composed with the three non-trivial sign patterns gives the three classical moves; the all-plus pattern is the parent map, each triple has a unique parent (`triple_unique_descent`) and exactly three children (`triple_child_count`) — the tree is ternary.
- **n = 3 finite generating set and completeness.** With the reflection, one sign change and the coordinate transpositions, every primitive Pythagorean quadruple with non-negative space coordinates and positive height is reachable from `(1,0,0,1)`, and reachability characterises primitivity exactly (`reach_of_prim`, `reach_iff_prim`). The associated groupoid acts transitively on primitive quadruples (`quadConnected_of_prim`).
- **Canonical spanning tree.** The all-plus reflection followed by absolute values is well-founded on primitive quadruples and reaches a height-one node (a permutation of the root) in finitely many steps (`canonStep_iterate_reaches_root`), so the quadruple graph does carry a canonical spanning tree.
- **Sharp growth constant.** The reflection move multiplies the height by at most `(√n+1)/(√n−1)` (`lorentz_move_height_bound`, proved by Cauchy–Schwarz; sharp at n = 3). This constant is algebraic of degree ≤ 2, a root of `(n−1)X² − 2(n+1)X + (n−1)` (`growth_const_quadratic`): `3+2√2 = (1+√2)²` for n = 2 (silver ratio squared) and `2+√3` for n = 3.
- **Hyperbolic boundary picture.** Normalising by the height sends quadruples to rational points of the unit sphere; the reflection acts there by `u ↦ (u − s + 1)/(2 − s)` with `s = (a+b+c)/d`, scaling the height by `2 − s` (`boundary_move`).

### Negative result — the conjecture fails in dimension 3
The quadruple graph is **not** a tree. A node can have two parents, but never more than two (`quad_at_most_two_descents`), and an explicit infinite two-parent family `(1, 2m, 2m², 2m²+1)` for m ≥ 2 is exhibited with both parents identified and shown reachable (`quad_two_parents_family`). The branching number is not constant: unique-parent and two-parent primitive quadruples both occur above any height (`quad_branching_not_constant`), so the number of children takes both 6 and 7 infinitely often (`quad_child_count_ge`).

The mechanism is a **harmonic branching law** (`quad_minus_descent_iff_rat`): a second parent, obtained by flipping the sign on coordinate `a`, exists precisely when `1/b + 1/c < 1/a` (equivalently `a(b+c) < bc`). Equality gives height-preserving "neutral" edges such as at `(1,2,2,3)` — a phenomenon impossible for triples, which is exactly why dimension 2 is a clean tree and dimension 3 is not.

### Other deliverables
`ComputationalEvidence.md` (small-case enumeration and the branching data behind the conjectures), `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` (five falsifiable next-cycle conjectures, each with a key-insight and why-now statement), and `SELF_EVALUATION.json` (quality 0.82, proof depth 0.80, novelty 0.72, grade "substantial"). None of the Phase A forbidden packaging files were created.

# Future Directions — Higher-Dimensional Pythagorean Trees

The work in `Catalog/Shared/HigherPythagorean/` settles the basic form of the hypothesis:

* the Berggren mechanism *does* generalise to Pythagorean quadruples — the all-ones Lorentz
  reflection `s_r` is integral exactly for `n = 2` and `n = 3` (`refl_not_integral_of_four_le`),
  it generates a groupoid acting transitively on primitive quadruples
  (`quadConnected_of_prim`), and the sharp one-step growth constant is the algebraic number
  `(√n+1)/(√n−1)` (`lorentz_move_height_bound`, `growth_const_quadratic`), equal to
  `3+2√2 = (1+√2)²` for triples and `2+√3` for quadruples;
* but the *tree* does **not** generalise: quadruple nodes may have two parents
  (`quad_two_parents_family`), never more (`quad_at_most_two_descents`), and the branching
  number takes both values `6` and `7` infinitely often (`quad_branching_not_constant`).
  Which case occurs is governed by an Egyptian-fraction condition `1/a > 1/b + 1/c`
  (`quad_minus_descent_iff_rat`).

The following conjectures are the natural next targets.

## Conjecture 1 (Density of two-parent nodes)

Among the primitive Pythagorean quadruples of height at most `X` (counted up to permutation and
sign), the proportion having two parents tends to a limit `δ ∈ (0,1)` as `X → ∞`, and `δ > 1/2`.

*Evidence.* The exhaustive enumeration in `ComputationalEvidence.md` gives `196/348 ≈ 0.563`
for `X = 80` (and `196/347 ≈ 0.565` excluding the root).

*The key insight is* that having a second parent is equivalent to the scale-invariant harmonic
inequality `1/a > 1/b + 1/c` on the normalised boundary point `(a,b,c)/d ∈ S²`, so the
proportion should be computable as the measure of an explicit spherical region against the
(known) equidistribution measure of primitive quadruples on `S²`.

*Why now?* The harmonic law (`quad_minus_descent_iff_rat`) turns a combinatorial question about
a tree into a measure computation on the ideal boundary — the boundary map is already formalised
(`sphere_of_quad`, `boundary_move`).

## Conjecture 2 (Exact growth exponent of the canonical spanning tree)

The all-plus reflection is a canonical parent map, so the quadruple graph carries a canonical
spanning tree rooted at `(1,0,0,1)`. Its node-counting function `N(X) = #{nodes of height ≤ X}`
satisfies `log N(X) / log X → 2`, and more precisely `N(X) ∼ κ X²` for an explicit `κ > 0`,
whereas the Berggren tree satisfies `N(X) ∼ κ₂ X` (linear).

*The key insight is* that the growth exponent should be the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set
of the reflection group acting on the boundary sphere `S²`, which for the (finite covolume)
group `O(3,1;ℤ)` is the full dimension `2` — while the triple case gives dimension `1`.

*Why now?* The annulus theorems (`quad_height_annulus`, `triple_height_annulus`) already pin the
multiplicative step to `[2−√3, 2+√3]`; only the counting remains.

## Conjecture 3 (Neutral edges and the star-line structure)

The set of *neutral* nodes — quadruples with `1/a = 1/b + 1/c` up to permutation, so that some
reflection preserves the height (`quad_neutral_move_iff`) — is exactly the set of nodes lying on
a "star line": for each such node, the orbit of the neutral reflection together with the
transpositions is finite, and the neutral nodes of height `≤ X` number `Θ(X^{1/2})`.

*The key insight is* that neutral edges are the fixed loci of an involution acting on the height
level sets, i.e. horizontal edges of the graph; they are the exact three-dimensional replacement
of the star lines of the Berggren corpus, which are empty in dimension two
(`triple_no_neutral_move`).

*Why now?* Both the neutral criterion and the smallest example `(1,2,2,3)` are already formal,
so the classification is a pure Diophantine problem `a(b+c) = bc`, `a²+b²+c² = d²`.

## Conjecture 4 (Higher dimensions: an integral group without an all-ones reflection)

For every `n ≥ 4` the group of integral automorphisms of `x₁²+…+xₙ² − y²` still acts with
finitely many orbits on primitive Pythagorean `n`-tuples, but no finite set of *reflections in
vectors of norm ≤ 2* generates a graph with a unique-parent structure; in fact for `n ≥ 5` the
number of parents of a node is unbounded as the height grows.

*The key insight is* that the failure already visible at `n = 3` (two parents) is caused by the
`n`-dependent constant in `s_r(v) = v − (2B(v,r)/(n−1))r`: the descending region on the boundary
sphere is a union of `n` caps whose overlap grows with `n`, and `n = 2` is the unique dimension
in which the caps are disjoint from all but one.

*Why now?* `refl_not_integral_of_four_le` shows the all-ones reflection leaves the lattice for
`n ≥ 4`, so a genuinely new generating set (Vinberg's algorithm for `O(n,1;ℤ)`) has to be
formalised — the natural next infrastructure step.

## Conjecture 5 (Kissing configurations from two-parent nodes)

Normalising the two parents of a two-parent quadruple gives two boundary points whose spherical
distance is bounded below by an absolute constant `c₀ > 0`; consequently the boundary points of
all nodes of height `≤ X` form a `c₀/X`-separated set, giving a sphere-packing (kissing-type)
lower bound of order `X²` for rational points of denominator `≤ X` on `S²`.

*The key insight is* that the height ratio annulus `[2−√3, 2+√3]` converts the arithmetic
separation of distinct parents into a metric separation on the ideal boundary.

*Why now?* `shadow_bound` and `boundary_move` already give the exact conformal factor `2 − s` of
each move, which is precisely the quantity controlling the separation.
